title: AMD EPYC 8005 SKU List and Value Analysis: Mainstream Sorano's Big Stride
gist: ServeTheHome's SKU analysis of AMD's EPYC 8005 'Sorano' family: seven Zen 5 SKUs from 8 to 84 cores on the SP6 socket with no feature gating, 6-channel DDR5-6400 (307GB/s) and 96 PCIe Gen5 lanes. The 8635P leads in throughput and efficiency (2.7W/core), the 16 and 24 core parts are best value under $50/core, and the 64 core 8535P is the worst at $86/core.

insights.claim: EPYC 8005 'Sorano' is AMD's mainstream server counterpart to the high-end EPYC 9005, bringing Zen 5 to a more modest platform and filling a significant hole in AMD's lineup.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Extends AMD's Zen 5 reach into lower-cost single-socket servers, competing for volume below the flagship tier.
insights.quote: The mainstream server counterpart to AMD’s high-end EPYC 9005 chips, Sorano filled a significant hole in AMD’s chip lineup
insights.locator: A few months back AMD launched their EPYC 8005

insights.claim: Versus the Zen 4-based EPYC 8004 Siena, Sorano has more cores, far higher clockspeeds and faster DDR5 support, using full-size Zen 5 cores rather than compact cores, which makes the SP6 platform far more capable and competitive.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Large generational uplift on the same socket makes drop-in upgrades viable and could drive refresh in edge and SMB servers.
insights.quote: With a larger number of cores, far higher clockspeeds, and support for much faster DDR5 memory, Sorano made AMD’s SP6 platform a far more capable and competitive offering in the market.
insights.locator: As we noted in our review at the time

insights.claim: The EPYC 8005 stack does not gate features by SKU: every chip from the 8 core 8025P to the 84 core 8635P gets 6 channels of DDR5 (including 2DPC), 96 PCIe Gen5 lanes and Zen 5, so buyers choose only on core count, power and second-order effects.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Simple SKU logic lowers selection friction and makes workload profiling the main purchase decision.
insights.quote: The mid-tier, single-socket server platform does not gate any features behind specific SKUs
insights.locator: For their first generation of 8000 series parts

insights.claim: Because the SP6 socket is shared with EPYC 8004, drop-in upgrades are viable, though some vendors are releasing new motherboards for Sorano anyway.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Socket continuity eases upgrades for existing SP6 installs; motherboard vendors still see new-board opportunity.
insights.quote: Drop-in upgrades are even a viable option here since AMD is using the same SP6 socket as with the EPYC 8004 generation
insights.locator: For potential customers, this simplifies the calculus

insights.claim: The seven SKUs span 8 to 84 Zen 5 cores because the SP6 IOD can connect up to 12 Zen 5 CCDs, and every SKU has a 4.5GHz maximum single-core turbo, a significant improvement over EPYC 8004.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Wide core range on one platform lets AMD address very different workloads with one validation base.
insights.quote: The SP6 IOD can be connected to up to 12 Zen 5 CCDs, so AMD has run the gamut here, with between 8 and 84 CPU cores.
insights.locator: Even with just 7 chip SKUs, however

insights.claim: All-core turbo clockspeeds are almost inverse to core count: the 84 core 8635P reaches just 3.45GHz, the 24 core 8225P 4.1GHz, and the 8 core 8025P higher still, with the 16 core 8125P an outlier at a lower all-core turbo than the 8225P.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Throughput-per-core and total throughput trade off; lightly threaded workloads favor small SKUs.
insights.quote: The 84 core EPYC 8635P offers an all-core turbo boost speed of just 3.45GHz
insights.locator: Taking a look at all-core turbo clockspeeds

insights.claim: The 84 core 8635P has a 225 Watt TDP and moving from a 64 core chip to 84 cores costs only 15 Watts at default TDPs, making it the most efficient at 2.7W per core versus a bit over 4.1W for the 48 core part and nearly 12W for the 8 core 8025P.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Uncore (IOD) power amortizes over more cores, so top-end SKUs win on energy efficiency per core, relevant to datacenter TCO.
insights.quote: this is a classic case of where the power costs of the uncore (or IOD, in this case) are getting amortized over fewer and fewer CPU cores

insights.claim: Higher-end Sorano chips cluster at around 200 Watts TDP, helped by their higher clockspeeds.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Similar power envelopes across upper SKUs simplify rack power planning.
insights.locator: AMD’s default TDPs vary from chip to chip

themes.theme: Cache and memory bandwidth per core

insights.claim: The 8635P has 384MB of L3 (just under 4.6MB per core) and the 64 core 8535P is the most cache-contested at 4MB per core thanks to 8 fully enabled CCDs, while the 8435P and 8225P have 5.3MB per core and the remaining three SKUs get 8MB per core.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Cache-sensitive workloads should target lower core-count SKUs with disabled cores per CCD.
insights.quote: it is the 64 core 8535P that is actually the most cache-contested chip here, at just 4MB per core

insights.claim: With no 3D V-Cache server part in this generation, the 8325P and similar SKUs are among the best options for highly threaded workloads that strongly benefit from extra L3 cache.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Absence of V-Cache SKUs leaves a gap AMD could fill later; for now mid-core SKUs serve cache-heavy needs.
insights.quote: Especially with AMD not producing 3D V-Cache server part in this generation

insights.claim: All seven SKUs share one 6-channel DDR5-6400 controller giving fixed 307GB/s platform bandwidth, so the 8 core 8025P gets about 38GB/s per core while the 84 core 8635P gets just 3.7GB/s per core.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Memory-bound workloads cannot benefit from high core counts on this platform; bandwidth per core falls inversely with cores.
insights.quote: With 307GB/second of memory bandwidth overall for the platform, the 8 cores on the 8025P get an ample 38GB/second each

insights.claim: At list price the 16 and 24 core SKUs are the best value at under $50 per core, versus $60+ per core for the others.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Value-oriented buyers should evaluate the 16 and 24 core parts first, subject to real-world discounts.
insights.quote: The best value here is found in the 16 and 24 core SKUs, which at list price are under $50 per core.
insights.locator: The best value here is found in the 16

insights.claim: The 64 core SKU is the weakest value at $86 per core, priced only a few hundred dollars below the 84 core top-end chip that costs $69 per core, while the 8 core SKU costs $66 per core.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Pricing anomaly pushes buyers who want high core counts straight to the 8635P rather than the 64 core part.
insights.quote: it works out to being $86 per core – a significantly higher price than any of the other SKUs.

insights.claim: Almost all server builds spend more on RAM than on the CPU itself, and nearly no one pays AMD's list prices, so SKU price-per-core scaling is inconsistent.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: CPU list price is a small part of platform cost; memory pricing drives total build economics.
insights.quote: almost all server builds are going to spend more on RAM to fill the server than they will the CPU itself
insights.locator: As AMD’s more budget-friendly server platform

insights.claim: No one-size-fits-all SKU exists in the EPYC 8005 stack: the 8635P is the throughput leader but has the highest cache and memory contention, while the 32 core 8325P ticks the most boxes as a jack-of-all-trades.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Customers must profile workloads; compute, memory and cost optima differ across the seven SKUs.
insights.quote: the 32 core 8325P does tick a lot of boxes here as a potential jack-of-all-trades
